findings.claim: The birds are fed extra corn in their last weeks, called gavage
findings.because: Gavage means force-feeding: corn is delivered by tube, several times a day, for about the last two weeks (ducks) to three or four weeks (geese). 'Fed extra corn' misdescribes it, and the card's own note says guests object to how it is produced; a server who calls it 'extra corn' gets caught out.
findings.fix: The birds are force-fed corn for their last two weeks, called gavage

findings.claim: tastes sweet and buttery, not like liver
findings.because: Foie gras still has a clear, mild liver flavor; it is far milder than lean liver, not free of it. A guest who dislikes liver and is told it does not taste of liver will be misled.
findings.fix: tastes sweet and buttery, only faintly of liver

findings.claim: Not chicken liver mousse or pâté, which blend a lean liver with butter.
findings.because: Pâté is a ground meat preparation (the roster's own Pâté card), often pork and not necessarily liver or butter-based; only the chicken liver mousse fits 'lean liver blended with butter'.
findings.fix: Not chicken liver mousse, lean liver whipped with butter, or pâté, a ground meat spread. This is the whole liver.

findings.claim: It always comes from farmed ducks or geese fattened on extra feed before slaughter.
findings.because: The 'extra feed' wording repeats the euphemism for force-feeding, and 'always' is overstated: a few producers, Eduardo Sousa's Spanish goose farm among them, make un-force-fed liver from geese that gorge naturally in autumn. That makes the trap partly true of a real product.
findings.fix: It comes from farmed ducks or geese, force-fed in their last weeks, not wild birds.

findings.claim: a centuries-old craft of southwest France
findings.because: Fattening goose liver goes back to ancient Egypt and Rome. It is now centered on southwest France, with Alsace the other great center, so calling it a craft of southwest France gets its origin wrong.
findings.fix: French for fat liver, an ancient craft now centered on southwest France

findings.claim: is still raised half wild, active and lean
findings.because: Most commercial guinea fowl are raised in barns or free-range systems like other farm poultry. 'Half wild' is not accurate, and it contradicts the card's own notThis, which says it is farmed like chicken. The lean, darker meat comes from the breed and a more active bird, not from wild rearing.
findings.fix: is a restless, active bird, naturally lean

findings.claim: Ducks fly and swim, so the breast is dark, red muscle
findings.because: The ducks served (Pekin, Moulard, Muscovy) are farm birds that barely fly. The red breast is inherited from wild ancestors that were strong fliers: the endurance muscle is rich in myoglobin. A guest can easily poke a hole in 'they fly'.
findings.fix: Ducks come from strong fliers, so the breast is dark, red muscle

findings.claim: usually farmed, cleaned and cooked ahead
findings.because: Much of the escargot sold is not farmed. The classic Burgundy snail (Helix pomatia) is mostly gathered wild in Central and Eastern Europe, and many tins hold giant African snails. Only the petit-gris is widely farmed. What holds true is that restaurants buy them cleaned and precooked, usually tinned.
findings.fix: bought cleaned and precooked, usually tinned

findings.claim: Enriched roll baked with sugar and egg and served with honey butter
findings.because: 'Enriched roll baked with sugar and egg' is nearly a true description of the roster's Brioche card, so this trap is a fair description of another card. A trap must not be true of another card.
findings.fix: Sweet yeast dough fried in lard and rolled in cinnamon sugar

findings.claim: Grits, grilled over wood, stuffed with sausage, glazed with honey or sorghum
findings.because: Pairs is for classic partners on a plate. 'Grilled over wood' is a cooking method, and 'stuffed with' and 'glazed with' are preparations, so a server reads the label as a list of partners and stumbles.
findings.fix: Grits, sausage stuffing, a honey or sorghum glaze, pepper jelly

findings.claim: They come from young veal and are neither sweet nor bread. Crisp outside, soft and creamy inside, and very mild, richer than any chicken.
findings.because: A guest asking 'what is that?' is asking what part of the animal it is, and this line never says. It only says what it is not, so the server is left without an answer to the follow-up question. 'Young veal' repeats itself, since veal is already a young animal. 'Richer than any chicken' is an odd comparison that tells the guest nothing about organ meat.
findings.fix: They're the thymus gland of veal, a mild organ meat, nothing like liver. Crisp outside, soft and creamy inside.

findings.claim: Most guests who try it order it again.
findings.because: This is an oversell a server cannot back up. Read aloud it sounds like a sales script. The line also never says plainly that this is the breast of a duck. It goes straight to a comparison.
findings.fix: It's the breast of the duck, served rosy and sliced like a steak, rich and tender under crisp, rendered skin.

findings.claim: tastes the way chicken used to, a little deeper and more savory, with firmer, leaner meat. Think chicken with a hint of pheasant.
findings.because: 'Tastes the way chicken used to' is a nostalgic claim the guest cannot check, and it sounds read off a card. 'A hint of pheasant' means nothing to a guest who has never eaten pheasant, and a nervous guest usually hasn't, so the comparison explains nothing.
findings.fix: It's a farm bird like chicken, but a little deeper and more savory, with firmer, leaner meat and just a faint wild note.

findings.claim: Seared foie gras, brioche, fig jam, sauternes
findings.because: Sauternes is a place name and a wine appellation, so a real menu capitalizes it. In lowercase it reads like a typo.
findings.fix: Seared foie gras, brioche, fig jam, Sauternes

findings.claim: Some guests object to how it is produced. Answer honestly and have another dish ready.
findings.because: The card never gives the doneness fact a server is asked most: seared foie gras is served rare to pink at the center, and a torchon or mi-cuit is only gently cooked, not cooked through. The why and guest line only say it melts inside.
findings.fix: Seared, it stays pink at the center, and a torchon is only gently cooked. Some guests object to how it is made, so answer honestly.

findings.claim: "quail", "often butter", "sometimes bacon"
findings.because: The pairs field names quail stuffed with sausage, which is a classic Southern preparation and usually pork. The madeWith list flags bacon but not the sausage stuffing, which also often holds bread crumbs.
findings.fix: "quail", "often butter", "sometimes bacon", "sometimes pork sausage"

findings.claim: "often wheat flour", "sometimes milk"
findings.because: Crispy or fried sweetbreads, like the menu line on this card, are often dredged in flour and then dipped in egg and bread crumbs. Egg is a guest-relevant ingredient the list leaves out.
findings.fix: "often wheat flour", "sometimes egg", "sometimes milk"

findings.claim: "chicken liver", "butter", "often shallot", "often brandy", "sometimes cream"
findings.because: A classic chicken liver parfait is bound with whole eggs and baked in a water bath. Both linked parfait recipes in this app use 3 to 4 eggs. Egg is missing from the list, so a server would not flag it for a guest with an egg allergy. Port or Madeira is also standard.
findings.fix: "chicken liver", "butter", "often egg", "often shallot", "often brandy or port", "sometimes cream"

findings.claim: creamy when cooked just to pink
findings.because: The card's own note says pink chicken liver is linked to food poisoning. USDA guidance is 74 C (165 F), and the UK FSA ties undercooked chicken liver pâté to Campylobacter outbreaks. The test answer should not endorse pink as the ideal.
findings.fix: Small, iron-rich chicken organ, silky and mild, often made into a spread

findings.claim: Cooked just to pink it stays creamy; cooked through it turns grainy.
findings.because: This teaches pink as the goal, which contradicts the note and US food-safety guidance. It is true that overcooking makes liver grainy. A parfait stays smooth because it is blended and gently baked in a water bath, not because it is served pink. The line also uses a semicolon.
findings.fix: Overcooked, it turns grainy, so kitchens cook it gently or bake it as a parfait.

findings.claim: so it needs three hours or more of simmering
findings.because: The origin line names gyutan, and gyutan is not simmered. Japanese grill bars peel the raw tongue, slice it thin and grill it quickly. Simmering for hours is usual for tacos and delis, but it is not a requirement of the cut.
findings.fix: so it is usually simmered three hours or more

findings.claim: Dense cow muscle simmered for hours, then peeled and sliced or seared
findings.because: Gyutan, which the card cites, is thin-sliced raw and grilled. The gist gives the long simmer as the defining trait, but it is only the most common way to cook the cut.
findings.fix: Dense, fatty cow muscle, usually simmered for hours, peeled and sliced

findings.claim: best cooked rare to medium rare
findings.because: Only the loin, the tenderloin and the leg steaks are served rare. Shoulder, shank and neck, which go into stews, osso buco and sausages, are braised well done. This deck's own recipe candidate is a venison stew.
findings.fix: Deep red, very lean deer meat, its loin best served rare to medium rare

findings.claim: It is at its best served rare to medium rare.
findings.because: This is true of the loin and steak cuts but false of braised or stewed venison. A server reading it at the table could tell a guest that a venison stew is served rare.
findings.fix: Loin and steaks are at their best rare to medium rare.

findings.claim: they eat like a lighter foie gras
findings.because: This oversells, and the card's own notThis says chicken liver is leaner and more mineral than foie gras. A guest who orders expecting foie gras gets something else, and the line blurs the confusion the card is meant to clear up.
findings.fix: Chicken livers are rich and silky, with a mild, slightly sweet iron flavor. Most often they are whipped with butter into a smooth spread for toast.

findings.claim: creamy when cooked just to pink
findings.because: The gist teaches a new hire that pink is the correct doneness, but the card's own note says pink chicken liver is linked to food poisoning and US guidance is 74 C (165 F). A server will repeat the gist to a guest as a promise about doneness.
findings.fix: Small, iron-rich chicken organ, creamy when cooked gently

findings.claim: roasted inside split leg pieces
findings.because: 'Split leg pieces' is vague: a test-taker cannot tell it means bones, and it could be read as meat. The gist needs to say where the fat sits, still without using the banned words.
findings.fix: Beef fat from a leg's hollow core, roasted and spread on toast

findings.claim: Organ meat with a strong, livery flavor and a soft, spreadable texture
findings.because: This is close to a true description of Chicken Liver or Pâté, both on the roster, so a test-taker who knows those cards could fairly argue for it. A trap must be false of every card.
findings.fix: Gristly, strong-tasting organ that stays chewy however long it cooks

findings.claim: Small farmed animal
findings.because: 'Animal' does not rule out the small farmed birds nearby (Guinea Hen, Quail), whose meat is also lean and mild. On a multiple-choice test this gist could be accepted for a bird. Naming it a mammal is what makes this one this one.
findings.fix: Small farmed mammal with lean, pale, mild meat, often braised

findings.claim: creamy when cooked just to pink
findings.because: The gist is drilled as the correct answer and teaches pink as the goal. The card's own note says pink chicken liver is linked to food poisoning and US guidance is 74 C (165 F). A server who learns the gist could tell a guest that pink is the right way to serve it.
findings.fix: Small, iron-rich chicken organ, silky unless it is overcooked

findings.claim: Cooked just to pink it stays creamy; cooked through it turns grainy.
findings.because: This presents undercooked liver as the correct doneness and cooked-through as a fault. That contradicts the note (a campylobacter risk; USDA says 74 C (165 F)). A server would repeat it as reassurance.
findings.fix: Overcooked, it turns grainy, so kitchens take care to keep it tender.

findings.claim: "chicken liver", "butter", "often shallot", "often brandy", "sometimes cream"
findings.because: The linked recipe is a parfait, and a classic baked chicken liver parfait is set with egg. Egg is a major allergen and the list leaves it out.
findings.fix: add "often egg"

findings.claim: "pheasant", "often butter", "often cream", "sometimes bacon", "sometimes apple brandy"
findings.because: The card's own line and pairs put chestnuts on the plate, and the US FDA lists chestnut as a tree nut. Bread sauce is also made with milk and wheat bread. The list names neither.
findings.fix: add "sometimes chestnut" and "sometimes bread"

findings.claim: (no note)
findings.because: Braised rabbit legs come on the bone and are full of small, fine bones. A server should say so plainly, especially to a guest ordering for a child. Nothing on the card mentions bones.
findings.fix: Braised legs come on the bone, and rabbit has many small, fine bones.

findings.claim: "often butter"
findings.because: The card's line and pairs both say mustard cream, but cream (milk) is not in madeWith.
findings.fix: add "sometimes cream"

findings.claim: Length parity: the gist (63 chars) is longer than both traps (58 and 60), so on this card the gist is the longest answer option. Every other card with traps has a trap at least as long as its gist.
findings.because: Length parity: the gist (63 chars) is longer than both traps (58 and 60), so on this card the gist is the longest answer option. Every other card with traps has a trap at least as long as its gist.
findings.fix: Shorten the gist, for example to "Calf thymus or pancreas, crisp outside and creamy within" (56 chars). That keeps both traps within about 4 characters of it and neither trap needs padding.

findings.claim: The Pheasant card (fd_0060) lists Guinea Hen under confusedWithTerms, and its notThis says the two birds both eat like a richer chicken. Guinea Hen does not link back: it lists Pheasant only under seeAlsoTerms. Its notThis also says it "eats far milder than pheasant or venison", which contradicts both cards. Guinea Hen's why says it has more flavor than chicken, and Pheasant's why says its flavor is only a little deeper than chicken, so the two cards put the birds at about the same level.
findings.because: The Pheasant card (fd_0060) lists Guinea Hen under confusedWithTerms, and its notThis says the two birds both eat like a richer chicken. Guinea Hen does not link back: it lists Pheasant only under seeAlsoTerms. Its notThis also says it "eats far milder than pheasant or venison", which contradicts both cards. Guinea Hen's why says it has more flavor than chicken, and Pheasant's why says its flavor is only a little deeper than chicken, so the two cards put the birds at about the same level.
findings.fix: Move Pheasant from seeAlsoTerms to confusedWithTerms, so seeAlsoTerms becomes ["Poussin"]. Rewrite the notThis to fit, for example: "Not pheasant, the long-tailed autumn game bird. Guinea hen is farmed like chicken and is far milder than venison." (about 110 chars, ends in a full stop).

findings.claim: Escargots, garlic parsley butter, grilled baguette
findings.because: The contract refused the dish line: it read "Escargots", and a line has to carry the term as written for say-it-back to find it on a menu.
findings.fix: The singular, as most American menus print it.

findings.claim: Not pheasant, the long-tailed autumn game bird. Guinea hen is farmed like chicken and is far milder than venison.
findings.because: The critic: the Pheasant card says the two birds eat alike, and this one called guinea hen far milder than venison, which is not the confusion a guest has.
findings.fix: Says what actually separates them (which bird it is), and agrees with the Pheasant card.

critic.notes: No other problems found. Every roster row has a card, and ids and terms match the roster exactly. The prose mean is 669 characters per card, under the 720 ceiling; the highest totals are Foie Gras at 794 and Chicken Liver at 771. The Quail packet error is covered: its trap reads "strong, gamy" and matches /gam[ey]|strong/i. I found no verdict words, no em or en dashes and no banned substrings. The one temperature is on Chicken Liver, 74 C (165 F), and it is correctly formatted. Every accented or hesitation term has a say (Escargot, Foie Gras, Poussin, Venison), and no gist uses its own term or a listed word from mayNotAppearInGistOrTraps. Foie Gras links to both Chicken Liver and Pâté, and Chicken Liver links back to Foie Gras. None of the traps (wild hare, wild boar, sea snails, mountain oysters, laying hen) describes another card on the roster. Two optional trims: Venison says rare to medium rare in its gist, guest line and note, so its note is the easy cut if the mean ever has to drop. Magret could take an optional say such as mah-GRAY, but it is an alias, not the term, so the card does not need one.

findings.claim: "beef tripe", "often tomato", "often onion", "sometimes white wine", "sometimes pecorino cheese", "sometimes hominy"
findings.because: Two of the three dishes the card names are classically made with pork. Callos a la madrilena is cooked with chorizo, morcilla and often ham or pig's trotter, and Mexican menudo is often made with pig's feet. A guest who avoids pork has to see that flagged, and the list has room for a seventh item.
findings.fix: Add "sometimes pork" as a seventh item: beef tripe, often tomato, often onion, sometimes white wine, sometimes pecorino cheese, sometimes hominy, sometimes pork

findings.claim: Hybrid duck breed raised for foie gras and a big red breast
findings.because: The moulard is a sterile first-generation cross of a Muscovy drake and a Pekin hen. It cannot breed true, so it is a hybrid and not a breed. The card's own why says so, but the gist, guest line and trap all call it a breed.
findings.fix: Sterile hybrid duck raised for foie gras and a big red breast

findings.claim: Moulard is the breed of duck raised for foie gras.
findings.because: It is a hybrid cross of two ducks, not a breed. A server who repeats "breed" will be corrected by any guest who raises ducks.
findings.fix: Moulard is the duck raised for foie gras, a cross of two breeds.

findings.claim: It is a breed, a sterile cross of Muscovy and Pekin ducks, not a place or a farm.
findings.because: A sterile cross is a hybrid, not a breed, so the explanation contradicts itself.
findings.fix: It is a duck, a sterile cross of Muscovy and Pekin, not a place or a farm.

findings.claim: Not Pekin, the smaller, milder Long Island breed behind most American duck breast and Peking duck.
findings.because: The Pekin breed comes from China and was brought to Long Island in 1873. "Long Island duck" is a name it is sold under, not where the breed comes from, so calling it a Long Island breed misstates its origin.
findings.fix: Not Pekin or Long Island duck, the smaller, milder bird behind most US duck breast and Peking duck.

findings.claim: (no aliases given)
findings.because: The same bird is printed on menus and sold as "Mulard" (the French spelling) and in English as "mule duck". Without these, a server who reads "Mulard duck breast" will not recognize it as this card.
findings.fix: "aliases": ["Mulard", "Mule Duck"]

findings.claim: The name is just for their shape.
findings.because: The guest line never says the word oyster or what shape is meant, so a guest who fears shellfish is left guessing, and a new hire has nothing plain to repeat. The brief puts this card at this level so the server can say plainly that the dish is chicken and not shellfish. It is longer than the words it replaces because a shellfish-allergy mix-up is a safety matter, and it states where the name comes from, not a verdict on what the dish holds.
findings.fix: The name is for their oyster shape, not the shellfish.

findings.claim: they eat like a tiny, tender steak with a rich dark-meat flavor, nothing like liver. They are usually grilled quick.
findings.because: Duck heart is dense muscle with a firm, springy chew. The card's own why says dense and its note warns about toughness, so calling it tender oversells it, and a guest expecting filet will be let down. "Grilled quick" also sounds casual and leaves out the pink finish the note describes.
findings.fix: they eat like a tiny steak, meaty with a slight chew and nothing like liver. Most are grilled fast and served pink.

findings.claim: It turns tender and mild and soaks up its sauce, like the heart of a good stew.
findings.because: "Like the heart of a good stew" tells the guest nothing about the texture, and texture is what a nervous guest is really asking about. Well-cooked tripe is soft but keeps a gentle, slightly bouncy chew. Saying plain "tender" oversells it.
findings.fix: It cooks soft with a gentle chew and a mild taste, and soaks up its sauce.

findings.claim: Not the shellfish. The name comes from the shape, a small oval like an oyster in its shell.
findings.because: This card exists so a server can answer a guest with a shellfish allergy, and the flat 'Not the shellfish' will be repeated at the table as 'there is no shellfish in it'. That is true of the cut, but not always of the plate. Chefs like the pun and sometimes serve chicken oysters with real oysters, oyster sauce or a seafood garnish. The card should say what the word means without vouching for the dish.
findings.fix: Not the shellfish: the name is only for the shape. The sauce or garnish can still hold seafood.

findings.claim: (no note)
findings.because: The Moulard breast, the magret on the card's own menu line, is classically seared and served pink, medium rare, and sliced. A server must be able to tell a guest that plainly before the order, because this is poultry served undercooked by default. Nothing on the card says it.
findings.fix: The breast is classically seared and served pink, medium rare, and sliced.

findings.claim: "beef tripe", "often tomato", "often onion", "sometimes white wine", "sometimes pecorino cheese", "sometimes hominy"
findings.because: The card's origin names callos in Madrid, which is classically cooked with chorizo, morcilla and pig's or calf's foot, and menudo often adds pig's foot. The madeWith list is the only place a guest who avoids pork would see it flagged, and it does not name pork. There is room for a seventh item.
findings.fix: add "sometimes pork" as a seventh item

findings.claim: Best seared fast to pink or braised long.
findings.because: When grilled, duck hearts come pink in the middle by default. 'Best' reads as the chef's taste, not as the doneness the guest will actually get, so a server would not know to say it plainly up front.
findings.fix: Grilled, they come pink in the middle. Cooked past that and not braised, they turn tough and rubbery.

findings.claim: Duck Hearts is confused with liver, and the card treats that as the main confusion: the guest line says "nothing like liver", the why says "closer to duck breast than to liver", and the only trap describes a livery organ. Chicken Liver (fd_0062) is still listed only in seeAlsoTerms, not in confusedWithTerms. The brief says that when the mistake is "people confuse it with X", the card should link X in confusedWithTerms and not rely on a trap. The trap also reads close to a description of liver, since chicken liver turns grainy when overcooked. Separately, the note repeats the guest line's "served pink". At 703 characters this is the second-longest new card.

critic.notes: Every roster row has a card: fd_0050 to fd_0063 are already written in src/lib/data/floor-deck.json, and this pass adds fd_0305 to fd_0308. Section prose mean with all 18 cards is 675.6, under the 720 ceiling. The new cards come to 622 / 703 / 683 / 760, every field is inside its band, and gist-to-trap length parity holds on all four. No banned substrings, verdict words, en/em dashes or degree signs in the new cards. The Quail knownPacketError is satisfied by the existing trap "Tiny wild-shot bird with a strong, gamy flavor and dark, livery meat". No gist or guest line duplicates an existing one, and the new gists are distinct from their neighbours (Tripe vs Beef Tongue, Moulard vs Duck Breast / Foie Gras). Facts checked and found sound: honeycomb tripe is the second chamber (reticulum); moulard is a sterile Muscovy drake x Pekin hen hybrid giving most foie gras, raised in southwest France and the Hudson Valley; the chicken oyster sits in the hollow of the ilium; sot-l'y-laisse means "the fool leaves it there". Cross-section linking: the roster has no Pekin, Muscovy, Chitterlings, Gizzard or Mountain Oysters card, so the notThis prose on Moulard and the trap on Tripe are the right tools. The Moulard why says "its breast, the magret", which is consistent with the Duck Breast card's Magret alias and origin line, so no confusion link is needed there. Operator: the shared scratchpad already held an unrelated new.json from another run; I wrote my measurement input to meats-critic-new4.json instead and left the existing file alone.

findings.claim: a truly wild bird from the Scottish moors, here only in the fall
findings.because: Red grouse is shot on moors across Britain, with a large share of the bag from northern England (Yorkshire, Durham, Northumberland), not only Scotland. The season opens 12 August and runs to 10 December, so the first and most prized birds arrive in late summer, not the fall.
findings.fix: a truly wild bird from the British moors, here only from mid-August into winter

findings.claim: Scottish moors, in season from 12 August, the Glorious Twelfth
findings.because: Red grouse are shot in Scotland and northern England; a server told only Scotland will be wrong when the kitchen's birds come from Yorkshire.
findings.fix: British moors, Scotland and northern England, in season from 12 August

findings.claim: "hare", "often red wine", "often bacon", "sometimes hare's blood", "sometimes port", "sometimes foie gras"
findings.because: Jugged hare and civet dredge the joints in flour before browning, and the card's own line is pappardelle, an egg and wheat pasta. A guest with a wheat or egg allergy gets no flag. Port is redundant once red wine flags alcohol.
findings.fix: "hare", "often red wine", "often bacon", "often wheat flour", "sometimes hare's blood", "sometimes egg", "sometimes foie gras"

findings.claim: Not rabbit, a farmed animal with pale, mild meat.
findings.because: Rabbit is also hunted wild (common in Britain and Europe). The real tells are species and meat color. Rabbit is usually farmed on US menus, but it is not farmed by definition.
findings.fix: Not rabbit, usually farmed, with pale, mild meat.

findings.claim: they have almost no muscle, so they eat soft and creamy
findings.because: Brain has no muscle at all. It is soft, fat-rich nerve tissue, and that fat and water, not a small amount of muscle, is why it eats creamy.
findings.fix: they are fatty nerve tissue, no muscle, so they eat soft and creamy

findings.claim: Not sweetbreads, the firmer thymus gland.
findings.because: Sweetbreads are the thymus or the pancreas, and menus sell both. Naming only the thymus contradicts what the Sweetbreads card teaches.
findings.fix: Not sweetbreads, the firmer thymus or pancreas.

findings.claim: "often wheat flour", "often capers", "sometimes vinegar", "sometimes lemon"
findings.because: Fried brains (Italian cervella fritta, the American brain sandwich, the breaded nose-to-tail fritter) are classically dipped in egg and crumbed, so egg needs a flag. The list has room for a seventh item.
findings.fix: add "sometimes egg"

findings.claim: The comb is mostly skin and connective tissue with little muscle.
findings.because: A comb holds no muscle at all. It is thickened skin whose core is collagen and hyaluronic-acid-rich tissue (combs are a commercial source of hyaluronic acid), and that tissue is why it braises gelatinous.
findings.fix: The comb is thick skin over collagen-rich tissue, with no muscle.

findings.claim: Ruffled red garden flower whose leaves are used as a garnish
findings.because: The trap's why says this describes celosia. Celosia is grown for its flowers, and its leaves are eaten as a cooked green, not as a garnish, so the why does not hold as written.
findings.fix: Ruffled red garden flower whose blooms are used as a garnish

findings.claim: Asked about mad cow? US rules bar brain only from cattle 30 months and older. Veal calves are a few months old.
findings.because: Framed as a scripted answer to a health worry, it tells the server to reassure the guest that the dish carries no risk. That is a safety verdict, which hard rule 1 forbids. The regulation is worth keeping as a fact, but the health question belongs to a manager or the kitchen, not to a third-day server.
findings.fix: US rules bar brain from cattle 30 months and older, and veal calves are months old. Send health questions to a manager.

findings.claim: They're poached, then browned in butter with capers.
findings.because: This states one classic preparation as tonight's fact. Kitchens also bread and fry brains, serve them with gribiche, or put them in ravioli. A server who repeats this line at a table where the dish is fried is wrong to the guest's face. The hare card hedges with "usually", and this one should too.
findings.fix: Usually poached, then browned in butter with capers.

findings.claim: they have almost no muscle
findings.because: Brain is nerve tissue, mostly water and fat, with no muscle at all. "Almost no muscle" leaves the server with the wrong picture when a guest asks why it is so soft.
findings.fix: they hold no muscle at all

findings.claim: gently poached in acidulated water
findings.because: "Acidulated" is kitchen jargon that a new hire cannot pass on. It means water sharpened with vinegar or lemon.
findings.fix: gently poached in vinegared water

findings.claim: the firmer thymus gland
findings.because: Sweetbreads can be either the thymus or the pancreas, and the deck's Sweetbreads card covers both. Naming only the thymus teaches half the fact.
findings.fix: the firmer glands

findings.claim: the boldest bird we serve
findings.because: This overclaims on behalf of a menu the card cannot see. The restaurant may serve no other bird, or a stronger one such as woodcock, so the server would be stating something false. The honest comparison is to the familiar birds.
findings.fix: bolder than pheasant

findings.claim: braised until soft and silky, often fried crisp
findings.because: Heard aloud, "soft and silky" and "fried crisp" sound like a contradiction. The guest needs the order: it is braised first, then crisped on the outside.
findings.fix: braised until silky, then often fried crisp outside

findings.claim: real chicken flavor
findings.because: This oversells by implying that ordinary chicken has no flavor, and a guest can push back on it. The honest claim is that the flavor is deeper.
findings.fix: deeper flavor

findings.claim: Asked about mad cow? US rules bar brain only from cattle 30 months and older. Veal calves are a few months old.
findings.because: The rule is stated correctly (FSIS bars brain as a specified risk material only from cattle 30 months and older). But putting the calves' age right after it implies the dish is safe, so a server ends up giving a medical assurance at the table. The card can state the rule, but a guest's health question should go to a manager.
findings.fix: US rules bar brain only from cattle 30 months and older. Send health questions to a manager.

findings.claim: Classic sauces are thickened with the hare's own blood. Ask the kitchen how tonight's is made.
findings.because: Hare, like the grouse on the card before it, is wild game that is usually shot, so lead shot can turn up in the meat. A server should be able to say that plainly. The grouse card does say it, and this card does not.
findings.fix: Wild and shot, so a stray pellet can turn up. Classic sauces are thickened with the hare's blood.

findings.claim: sometimes bread
findings.because: Bread sauce and the fried bread croute under a roast grouse are both made from wheat bread. A guest who avoids wheat needs to hear the grain named, and 'bread' alone does not name it.
findings.fix: sometimes wheat bread

critic.notes:
I checked the five new cards (fd_0360 to fd_0364) against every rule, and each passes on its own. The roster is complete: all 23 rows have cards. Every field is inside its range. No verdict words, dashes or banned strings. Each trap is within 10 characters of its gist, and no gist is the longest option. No gist or guest line repeats. The section mean is fine: the new five average 705 characters of prose and all 23 cards average 681, against the 720 ceiling. The Quail packet error already has its matching trap (\"strong, gamy... livery\"). I checked the Blue Foot facts against Wikipedia: British Columbia, Peter Thiessen, from the 1980s, 14 to 16 weeks, white bird with a red comb and steel-blue feet. One source says 17 weeks, so \"more than twice as long\" holds either way.

All five problems are on cards that were already written. Adding the new terms made them stale, and the earlier authors could not have seen it.

Smaller points, for the operator to decide:
(1) Calf's Brains: the gist says \"seared in brown butter\" but the origin says \"au beurre noir\", which is black butter, and the madeWith lists vinegar. Both are fine for American menus, but \"seared in browned butter\" or simply \"pan-seared\" would remove the mismatch.
(2) Cockscomb's guest line compares it to braised pork skin and its why compares it to a pig's trotter. Picking one would be tidier.
(3) Cockscomb's line uses \"sauce gribiche\", and Gribiche (fd_0334) is a card. It could go in seeAlso if one of the current three gives way.
(4) Placing Blue Foot Chicken at level 4 is arguable. It shows up on good American menus more often than grouse or cockscomb, and \"needs a sentence to explain\" fits level 3. The meats levels would then be 4:6 and 3:6.
(5) Grouse could add Partridge or Woodcock as aliases or cards in a later expansion. Neither is on the 400-card roster.
